Imagine dragging a rough, jagged rock across a wooden surface. That harsh, scratchy, grating action — and the unpleasant sound it makes — is the heart of what "rasp" means. Once you feel that image, everything else will click.

1. To scrape or rub something with a rough, coarse surface

When you rasp something, you are scraping it hard with a rough tool or rough surface, wearing it down or shaping it in the process. The action is never smooth or gentle — it is always coarse, grinding, and abrasive.

"She rasped the wood with a metal file until the surface was even."
"He rasped the old paint off the wall."
"The cook rasped the block of hard cheese over the grater."

Notice that in all these examples, material is being removed or shaped through rough, repeated scraping. You can almost feel the friction.

2. To speak, or to make a sound, in a harsh and grating way

This is the more commonly used meaning in everyday language. When someone rasps something, they say it in a rough, scratchy, hoarse voice — the kind of voice that sounds dry, strained, and uncomfortable to listen to. Think of a person who has been screaming for hours, or someone with a severely sore throat, or a villain in a movie speaking in a low, rough growl.

"Get out of my house," he rasped.
"She was so sick that she could only rasp a few words before falling silent."
"The old man rasped her name from across the room."

This meaning also extends beyond the human voice. Any object that produces a harsh, scraping, grating sound can be said to rasp:

"The rusty gate rasped loudly as it swung open."
"His boots rasped against the stone floor as he walked."
"The saw rasped through the thick branch."
How the Two Meanings Are Connected

You might be wondering — what does scraping wood have to do with a rough voice? The connection is the quality of the sensation. Both feel the same way: coarse, harsh, and grating. Just as a rough file scraping across metal creates an unpleasant, grinding friction, a rasping voice creates an unpleasant, grinding sound. The word carries the same rough, abrasive energy in both cases. It is never soft, never smooth, never pleasant.
The Degree and Tone of the Word

"Rasp" is not a neutral word. It almost always suggests something that is uncomfortable — either to the ears, to the touch, or to the nerves. When a writer chooses "rasp" over a simpler word like "say" or "scrape," they are deliberately signaling:

  • Roughness — the texture or sound is coarse, not smooth
  • Strain or effort — something is being forced, worn down, or squeezed out
  • Discomfort — either for the speaker, the listener, or both

This makes it a very expressive and vivid word. Writers use it to make a scene feel raw and tense.

There is also a common phrase: to rasp on someone's nerves (or simply to rasp on), meaning to irritate someone continuously, to grate on them emotionally.

"His constant complaining rasped on her nerves."
"The noise rasped on until she could no longer concentrate."

Here, the word works metaphorically — just as physical rasping scrapes away at a surface, this kind of behaviour scrapes away at a person's patience.

——
PhysicalTo scrape or grind something with a rough surface, wearing it down
Sound / VoiceTo speak, or to produce a sound, that is harsh, scratchy, and grating
Emotional (phrase)To rasp on = to irritate continuously, to grate on someone's nerves
One Final Way to Remember It

Whenever you see or hear the word rasp, ask yourself: Is something rough scraping against something else? If the answer is yes — whether that "scraping" is physical, acoustic, or emotional — then "rasp" is exactly the right word for it.
